newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwandan suspect pleads not guilty to genocide.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan suspect pleads not guilty to genocide.

text.p: Former Rwandan army colonel Theoneste Bagosora on Friday pleaded not guilty to genocide and crimes against humanity before the U.N. tribunal on the 1994 mass slaughter.
The most prominent Rwandan suspect in tribunal custody, Bagosora, 56, wearing a dark blue suit, appeared before the tribunal at its headquarters in this northern Tanzanian town.
He looked confident and told the court he was a married father of seven and worked with the Rwandan armed forces.
He pleaded not guilty to genocide, crimes against humanity and two counts of violations of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 on the protection of war victims and additional protocols.
The court then met in private to set a date for his trial.
He was represented by defence lawyer Banjamin Ondingui of Cameroon but has requested he be defended by Luc de Temmerman of Belgium. The tribunal has not yet ruled on the request.
Bagosora, cabinet director in the former defence ministry, assumed de facto control of events in Rwanda in the first few days of the genocide, according to the prosecution indictment.

An estimated 800,000 members of the Tutsi minority and Hutu political moderates were killed in the three-month genocide by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs after the killing of Rwanda's Hutu president.
Bagosora was brought from Cameroon for trial with four other indicted genocide suspects in January. The three other suspects pleaded not guilty to genocide and crimes against humanity last month.
In another development, the tribunal postponed until May 12 the trial of former mayor Jean Paul Akayesu to give time for the defence to prepare after the prosecution completed its case.
The last prosecution witness was a 26-year-old Tutsi woman who said she lived in Taba commune, where Akayesu was mayor, and hid in the commune offices for three days during the genocide.
The woman, known as Witness H, said she was raped by a member of the Hutu extremist Interhamwe militia before hiding in the offices where other militiamen raped and molested women and young girls.
"Sometimes the militiamen told passing men to come and pick young girls from where we were, register their names and then the men could take them away, after which they were all killed," she said.
She said she witnessed three rapes and could remember names of 10 men who raped women who had taken refuge in the offices.
"Sometimes they raped women right there on sight while sometimes they took them to the nearby bush," said witness H.
"If Akayesu wanted he could have prevented these events from taking place because he was the mayor of that commune but by not protecting us from all these events he participated in them," she said.
Akayesu, 43, who is held in Arusha since last May, has pleaded not guilty to genocide and crimes against humanity. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment, the tribunal's highest penalty.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan dismissed two top tribunal officials late last month after a scathing U.N. report detailed administrative mismanagement, unqualified staff and legal chaos.
